books.title: Amadís de Gaula
books.author: Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo
books.chapterVerdict: In Part I, Chapter 6, the priest calls Amadís the source from which the other Spanish books of chivalry descend, but the barber argues it is the best of its kind. It is spared for the moment.
books.literaryInfluence: Amadís gave early modern readers a model of the perfect wandering knight: brave, refined, loyal to Oriana, and seemingly built for endless adventure. Don Quixote imitates that literary template so completely that reading becomes behavior.
books.realWorldConsequence: By Cervantes's lifetime, armored knight-errantry belonged more to print culture than to practical warfare. The comedy comes from watching an old literary code collide with roads, inns, muleteers, debts, and ordinary bodies.
books.readingQuestion: When does admiration for a story become an attempt to live inside it?
books.sourceNote: Britannica dates the first known Montalvo version to 1508; Chapter 6 preserves the book in the library trial.

books.title: Las Sergas de Esplandián
books.author: Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo
books.chapterVerdict: The priest refuses to let the merit of Amadís protect its sequel. The housekeeper throws Esplandián into the yard to start the bonfire.
books.literaryInfluence: The sequel extends the Amadís universe through crusading fantasy, enchanted geography, and the heroic son of the famous knight. It shows how successful romances became sprawling franchises.
books.realWorldConsequence: The book's imagined island of California, ruled by Queen Calafia, is the most famous reminder that chivalric fantasy traveled with exploration and conquest. Most historians describe the name California as likely deriving from this romance.
books.readingQuestion: Why would a book of impossible islands matter to people crossing the Atlantic?
books.sourceNote: Chapter 6 condemns Esplandián; the California connection is usually phrased as likely rather than absolutely certain.

books.title: Palmerín de Inglaterra
books.author: Francisco de Moraes
books.chapterVerdict: The priest saves Palmerín de Inglaterra and compares its preservation to keeping Homer in a precious case.
books.literaryInfluence: Cervantes lets the priest admire its clarity, proportion, and well-managed adventures. It becomes proof that the novel is not simply anti-book; it is anti-bad-reading and anti-formula.
books.realWorldConsequence: The contrast with Spain's costly wars and fiscal strain makes the polished fantasy feel both seductive and evasive. Good style cannot make a vanished social order return.
books.readingQuestion: Why does Cervantes save some fantasies while mocking the fantasy habit itself?
books.sourceNote: The Chapter 6 verdict distinguishes Palmerín de Inglaterra from Palmerín de Oliva.

books.title: Palmerín de Oliva
books.author: anonymous or uncertain
books.chapterVerdict: The priest orders Palmerín de Oliva burned so thoroughly that no ashes remain, immediately before praising Palmerín de Inglaterra.
books.literaryInfluence: As the first Palmerín romance, it helped launch another popular chivalric cycle. Its presence beside Palmerín de Inglaterra makes the library scene feel like literary criticism disguised as household triage.
books.realWorldConsequence: The episode teaches first-time readers to notice Cervantes's selectivity. He is not attacking all imagination; he is sorting lively art from mechanical imitation.
books.readingQuestion: What makes one adventure worth preserving and another disposable?
books.sourceNote: Wikisource notes the 1511 Salamanca printing; Chapter 6 sends it to the fire.

books.title: Tirant lo Blanch
books.author: Joanot Martorell and Martí Joan de Galba
books.chapterVerdict: The priest calls Tirant a treasury of pleasure and, in its style, the best book in the world, while still teasing its author for deliberate foolishness.
books.literaryInfluence: Tirant mixes romance with surprisingly practical details: knights eat, sleep, make wills, and operate in political and military systems. That realism helps explain why Cervantes singles it out.
books.realWorldConsequence: Tirant points toward the kind of modern prose fiction Don Quixote will become: funny, material, self-aware, and unwilling to let pure fantasy float away from ordinary life.
books.readingQuestion: Why is a more realistic chivalric romance funny in a different way?
books.sourceNote: Biblioteca Virtual Miguel de Cervantes highlights Cervantes's praise and the 1490 Valencia publication.

books.title: Belianís de Grecia
books.author: Jerónimo Fernández
books.chapterVerdict: The priest says Don Belianís and its continuations need purging of excess, then tells the barber to keep them where nobody will read them.
books.literaryInfluence: Belianís represents the inflation of chivalric spectacle: bigger episodes, more continuations, more verbal heat. Don Quixote loves precisely this kind of overcharged heroic energy.
books.realWorldConsequence: The joke lands because excess was not just literary. Cervantes's Spain knew imperial overextension, status anxiety, and grand claims running ahead of material capacity.
books.readingQuestion: How does a culture sound when it keeps raising the volume on glory?
books.sourceNote: The Centro Virtual Cervantes notes Belianís as a real chivalric book associated with the library scrutiny.

books.title: Olivante de Laura
books.author: Antonio de Torquemada
books.chapterVerdict: The priest dismisses Don Olivante de Laura as a swaggering fool and sends it into the yard.
books.literaryInfluence: Olivante shows the late-stage appetite for elaborate heroes, invented kingdoms, and impossible promotion. It is exactly the sort of grandiose material Alonso Quijano turns into a life plan.
books.realWorldConsequence: Cervantes places inflated literary rank beside the ordinary household labor of a niece and housekeeper. The fantasy of status literally gets handled like clutter.
books.readingQuestion: What happens when status is easier to print than to earn?
books.sourceNote: Centro Virtual Cervantes identifies Olivante de Laura as a 1564 chivalric book by Antonio de Torquemada.

books.title: Felixmarte de Hircania
books.author: Melchor Ortega
books.chapterVerdict: In the Ormsby translation, the book appears as Florismarte of Hircania; the priest condemns the stiffness and dryness of its style.
books.literaryInfluence: Felixmarte piles marvel on marvel but is mocked for making wonder feel dry. Cervantes is interested in the reader's appetite, but also in literary craft.
books.realWorldConsequence: The book helps first-time readers see that Don Quixote is not only about believing false things. It is about what bad style can do to judgment, taste, and self-image.
books.readingQuestion: Can a boring fantasy be more dangerous than an exciting one?
books.sourceNote: Centro Virtual Cervantes identifies Felixmarte de Hircania as a 1556 work by Melchor Ortega.
